slides.title: Page tables
slides.sub: 4 levels of 9 bits and a 12-bit offset
slides.main: The guest keeps its own tables, but the processor needs real addresses.

captions: The address splits into four 9-bit indexes and a 12-bit offset
Each index selects an entry in the next-level table
The table root is set by CR3, which holds a guest physical address
One table is not enough: a translation to the host address is needed too

slides.title: Shadow tables
slides.sub: Shadow: guest address straight to host
slides.main: Guest edits to its tables are intercepted, the shadow is updated.

captions: The guest keeps its table, while the hypervisor knows how guest and host addresses match
The hypervisor builds a shadow that translates the guest address straight to the host one
Pages with guest tables are write-protected: an edit causes an exit
The real CR3 gets the shadow, not the guest table

slides.title: Cost of shadows
slides.sub: Every mapping edit is an exit
slides.main: Shadows are costly to run and complex in code.

captions: Creating processes, launching programs, and allocating memory change mappings
Each such operation turns into exits to the hypervisor
Shadows take extra memory
The state of the shadows must match the guest tables exactly

slides.title: EPT and NPT
slides.main: The guest keeps its own, the hypervisor the nested ones; hardware does the walk.

captions: The guest keeps the first table: guest virtual → guest physical
The hypervisor keeps the second: guest physical → host (EPT on Intel, NPT on AMD)
The processor walks both tables in a row
A guest table edit causes no exit; editing the nested ones is the hypervisor's job

frames.text: the guest edits its tables — no exits at all

slides.title: Two-dimensional walk
slides.main: On a TLB miss the processor makes (4+1)×(4+1)−1 accesses.

captions: Without virtualization the walk is four memory accesses
Each guest step yields a guest physical address that is itself translated in four steps
Five rows of five accesses minus one: 24
So a translation cache miss is especially costly in virtualization

slides.title: TLB and tags
slides.main: Ready translations in the TLB save you from the 2D walk.

captions: The TLB holds ready translations straight to the host address
On a miss both tables must be walked
Guest tags avoid flushing the cache on every switch
The processor also stores intermediate results of walks

frames.text: entries tagged VPID/ASID need no flush

slides.title: Huge pages
slides.main: A big page: shorter walk, wider TLB reach.

captions: An ordinary page: full four-level walk
A 2 MiB page removes one level
A 1 GiB page removes two levels
One TLB entry covers hundreds of times more memory

slides.title: EPT violation
slides.main: The hypervisor gets control on an access to a missing mapping.

captions: If the mapping exists, access proceeds without the hypervisor
No entry or wrong permissions — exit with the reason "violation"
The hypervisor allocates, swaps in, copies, or emulates a device
The entry appears and the guest repeats the access

slides.title: Shadow vs nested
slides.sub: What to choose and what to do
slides.main: Nested tables by default; give guests huge pages.

captions: Shadow tables: fast walk, but every edit is an exit
Nested tables: cheap edits, but an expensive TLB miss
Modern processors chose nested tables; KVM enables them by default
Give guests huge pages and watch the TLB miss rate
